extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, patent applicants, and practitioners evaluating §101 patent eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance enumerating categories of 'abstract ideas' used in §101 patent-eligibility analyses (Alice/Mayo framework), with descriptions and case-law examples showing how courts have treated each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to certain business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to business practices such as generating menus, generating a second menu from a first and sending it to another location, taking orders from restaurant customers, structuring a sales force or marketing company, using advertising as an exchange/currency, or algorithms for business optimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have described such claims as directed to abstract ideas — e.g., adding conventional computer components to well-known business practices does not make them patent-eligible. Representative cases: Enfish-era examples including claims described as “generating menus … or taking orders from restaurant customers,” In re Ferguson (structuring a sales force), Ultramercial v. Hulu (advertising as currency), In re Maucorps (algorithm for visit scheduling). The guidance emphasizes that merely implementing business practices on generic computers or adding conventional components is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to managing human behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that address methods of managing or influencing human behavior, such as storing user-selected spending limits and notifying users (budgeting/tracking financial transactions), filtering content, or mental processes a specialist should follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have treated such concepts as abstract ideas because they are methods of organizing human activity (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One Bank—tracking transactions to determine preset spending limits; BASCOM—filtering content as an abstract idea though eligibility turned on step 2B analysis). Examples include rules for user behavior monitoring and mental processes (In re Meyer). The guidance notes similarity to other methods of organizing human activity found abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to tracking or organizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to filtering, classifying, collecting, analyzing, encoding/decoding, organizing, receiving/screening/distributing, or otherwise structuring information (including tailoring content based on user data or navigation data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly characterized such information-management concepts as abstract ideas (e.g., BASCOM—filtering content; Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One—customizing web pages; TLI Communications—classifying and storing digital images; Electric Power Group—collecting/analyzing/displaying results; RecogniCorp—encoding/decoding images; Digitech—organizing through mathematical correlations; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec—email screening/distribution). The guidance highlights that information is intangible and that collecting/analysing/presenting information without more is within the realm of abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: An idea 'of itself' (uninstantiated concepts and mental processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas standing alone—uninstantiated concepts, plans, schemes—or mental processes that can be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts label such uninstantiated concepts and purely mental processes as abstract and non-patentable (CyberSource; Gottschalk v. Benson). The guidance explains that methods performable mentally or by humans with pen and paper are basic tools open to all, and that claims requiring only generic computer components but otherwise claiming mental work remain abstract. Presenting results of abstract collection/analysis without identifying a particular tool for presentation is also abstract (Content Extraction; Ultramercial; Electric Power Group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to data comparisons performable mentally or analogous to human mental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that involve obtaining, collecting, comparing, or mapping intangible data and determining validity or differences—steps that a human could perform mentally or with pen and paper (e.g., verifying credit-card validity by comparing transaction data; comparing genetic sequences to identify alterations; anonymous loan shopping comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed data-comparison steps can be performed in the human mind or with routine pen-and-paper techniques, courts have found them to be abstract mental processes (e.g., CyberSource—map of transactions to verify validity; University of Utah v. Ambry Genetics—comparing BRCA sequences; Mortgage Grader—anonymous loan shopping). The guidance notes that claims not requiring network or computer implementation may read on purely mental performance and thus be ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to organizing or analyzing information performable mentally or analogous to human mental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite converting, translating, recognizing, analyzing, or otherwise organizing information in ways that read on mental processes (e.g., translating functional descriptions to hardware descriptions, data recognition and storage, detecting misuse by collecting/analyzing access logs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found such claims abstract where the steps could be performed mentally or are equivalent to longstanding human practices (Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics—translating circuit descriptions; Content Extraction—data collection/recognition/storage; FairWarning—collecting/analyzing access logs and notifying). The guidance stresses that merely invoking computer-based tools in the specification is insufficient if the claims themselves do not require computer implementation or otherwise add meaningful technological improvements (distinguishing from claims that improve computer functionality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts described as ideas having no particular concrete or tangible form
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting conceptual frameworks or building-block ideas without a particular concrete application or tangible form (e.g., using advertising as currency, determining prices via organizational/product hierarchies, assigning hair designs to balance head shape).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have characterized such high-level conceptual frameworks as abstract ideas because they lack concrete/tangible application and are basic conceptual building blocks for organizing information (Ultramercial—advertising as currency; Versata—determining price with hierarchies; In re Brown—hair-cutting allocation). The guidance shows that abstractness can arise even when practical steps are recited if the claim is essentially a non-concrete conceptual scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships/formulas (judicial exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts including algorithms, mathematical relationships, formulas, and calculations are treated as judicial exceptions (abstract ideas or akin to laws of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance explains that courts have long regarded mathematical formulas and algorithms as non-statutory exceptions (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr). Mathematical procedures are treated as abstract ideas; whether a claim that uses a formula is patent-eligible depends on whether additional claim elements amount to significantly more than the abstract mathematical concept (see Alice/Mayo framework). Examples include converting binary-coded decimals, formulae for alarm limits, and mathematical hedging formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to a mathematical relationship or formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite or are rooted in a specific mathematical formula or relationship (e.g., Arrhenius equation for cure time in Diehr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have treated specific mathematical formulas as judicial exceptions (Diehr noted an Arrhenius equation as an exception like a law of nature). The guidance reiterates that asserting a mathematical relationship alone is not sufficient for patent eligibility; the presence of a formula calls for careful step-two analysis to determine whether the claim adds an inventive concept beyond the mathematical relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that involve calculating, manipulating numeric values, generating derived values, or organizing information through mathematical correlations (e.g., life-insurance policy value calculations, data manipulation using mathematical formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found claims directed to mere mathematical computation or manipulation to be abstract (Bancorp—policy value calculations as mere computation; Digitech—manipulating existing information with formulas to create new forms). Representative examples include algorithms for visit-optimization, algorithms for detecting abnormal conditions by calculation, and other calculation-based processes. The guidance emphasizes that mathematical calculation alone does not render a claim patent-eligible absent additional limitations that provide a specific, practical application or technological improvement.
